_note: Learn mode. One lesson per NASA hazard and moment of the mission. Facts are paraphrased from the linked NASA page. 'basis' says what the fact rests on: 'iss' = learned from long missions on the space station, 'expected' = what NASA expects for Mars, 'fact' = measured fact about Mars. 'importance' (1-3) feeds the max-heap that picks the top topics of a month. Months follow stages.json (Mars stay = months 9-27).

lessons.title: Leaving Earth's gravity
lessons.text: In the first days without gravity, your inner ear gets mixed signals, so dizziness and motion sickness are common. From space station crews, NASA has learned that the body adapts over time.
lessons.sourceName: NASA HRP · Sensorimotor and vestibular function

quiz.q: Which part of the body gets confused first without gravity?

lessons.title: Months of floating: bones and muscles
lessons.text: When your legs don't carry your weight, bones and muscles start to weaken. That's why astronauts on the space station exercise every day.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts exercise every day?

lessons.title: Landing in 38% gravity
lessons.text: Gravity on Mars is only 38% as strong as on Earth. After months of floating, your balance has to adapt again, so the first steps on Mars can feel strange. NASA calls these changes between gravity fields one of the 5 hazards.

quiz.q: How strong is gravity on Mars compared with Earth?

lessons.title: A Mars day is 24 h 39 min
lessons.text: A day on Mars lasts 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds. That extra time every day can shift your body clock, and NASA lists sleep loss and irregular schedules as a spaceflight risk. Regular light and sleep times help.
lessons.sourceName: NASA JPL · Mars at a Glance

quiz.q: How long is a day on Mars?

lessons.title: Help is up to 22 minutes away
lessons.text: A message between Earth and Mars takes from 0 up to about 22 minutes each way, depending on where the planets are. Doctors on Earth can't answer in real time, so the crew has to check their own health first. That's why the self-check matters.
lessons.sourceName: NASA NTRS · Communication Delays for Crewed Mars Missions

quiz.q: Why do Mars crews need to check their own health?
options: Messages to Earth can take up to ~22 minutes
There is no doctor on Earth

lessons.title: Outside Earth's protective bubble
lessons.text: Earth's magnetic field works like a bubble that shields us from most space radiation. Missions to Mars go beyond that bubble, so NASA is developing radiation shielding to protect crews. Radiation is invisible, which makes it one of the hardest hazards.

quiz.q: What protects us from most space radiation on Earth?

lessons.title: Living in 3/8 gravity for up to two years
lessons.text: NASA says Mars crews would live and work in three-eighths of Earth's gravity for up to two years. Muscles, bones and organs keep adjusting to that load, so exercise continues on Mars too.

quiz.q: How long could a crew live in Mars gravity, according to NASA?

lessons.title: Same crew, small habitat
lessons.text: Living for months or years in a small habitat with the same few people can affect mood, stress and teamwork. NASA says Mars crews must be carefully chosen, trained and supported. Talking with your crew and keeping a diary help.

quiz.q: What helps with isolation on a long mission?
options: Talking with the crew and keeping a diary

lessons.title: Eyes and brain on long missions
lessons.text: On long space station missions, NASA has seen changes in the structure of some astronauts' eyes and brain, called SANS. Blurry vision is something to report to the crew and in your next report to Earth.

quiz.q: What should you do if your vision gets blurry?
options: Tell the crew and report it

lessons.title: Dust and a closed habitat
lessons.text: The habitat is home and machine at once: temperature, pressure, air and microbes must all be controlled. NASA has studied how fine dust on other worlds, like the Moon, can affect lungs, eyes and skin, so keeping dust out of the habitat matters.

quiz.q: Which body parts can fine dust affect?

lessons.title: The immune system in a closed world
lessons.text: NASA studies how spaceflight changes the immune system. In a closed habitat, monitoring microbes and how the crew's bodies respond is part of keeping everyone healthy.

quiz.q: What does NASA monitor to protect the immune system in a habitat?

lessons.title: Heading home: heart and fitness
lessons.text: On the way back, the body is in microgravity again. NASA studies how the heart, blood vessels and fitness change in space, so the crew keeps exercising to be ready for Earth's gravity.

quiz.q: Why keep exercising on the trip home?
options: To be ready for Earth's gravity

lessons.title: Back on Earth: full gravity again
lessons.text: After about three years away, the body has to adjust to Earth's full gravity again. Balance, muscles and bones all take time. NASA counts this last change of gravity as part of the same hazard.

quiz.q: How long would a Mars mission keep the crew away from Earth?
